paras: The Henderson County abduction of an unknown white man was an episode in Henderson County, North Carolina, in early August 1888, in which five Black men reportedly beat a white man senseless and carried him off with a rope. The man was not seen again, five men were jailed at Hendersonville, and the white press reported the case as a lynching "by negroes." A body later seen in the French Broad River near Asheville was supposed to be his, but it was never recovered.

The victim was described only as an unknown white man "supposed to be from Yancey county." The account of what happened came from Henry Sumner, a Black man who was himself jailed and described as "a witness of the affair."

According to Sumner, two white men met three Black women, among them Lottie Corpening, whom the dispatch called "a notorious prostitute." A quarrel followed in which one of the men knocked Corpening down, and all three women then attacked the two men. One man fled, but his companion was still being beaten when five Black men came up, beat him "into insensibility," fetched a rope from a nearby house and took him away. One of the men reportedly told another Black man that the party had "treated him like they treated that negro over in Asheville."

William Carpening, John Ramsey, George King, Abraham King and Sumner were arrested and jailed at Hendersonville, and a search party combed the woods and creeks amid "considerable excitement." On August 22 two Black women fishing near Asheville saw a white man's body floating down the French Broad, and Police Chief F. N. Waddell searched the river and telegraphed towns downstream, without result. No report of the body's recovery, an inquest or a trial of the jailed men was found in the coverage.

The Richmond Dispatch carried the first report in a Raleigh news roundup under the heading "A LYNCHING," retelling Sumner's account at length. The Asheville Citizen called the floating body "A SENSATION" and headlined it as "Supposed to be the Man that was Lynched by Negroes in Henderson County," referring to the Black witnesses as "darkies." A second Dispatch telegram reduced the case to the man "lynched by negroes" for "an alleged assault upon a negro woman," a motive the first report did not state.

Witnesses at Asheville disagreed about the body: William Lyda and Noah Weldon said its arms seemed tied to the trunk, while a young white man named Davis said the arms and hands stuck up out of the water.

bases: Both papers called the episode a lynching of a white man by Black men: five men beat him senseless and took him away with a rope, and he was not seen again (A1, A2, A3).

Five men acting without legal authority beat the man and took him away with a rope, and the press treated him as lynched (A1, A3), but no body was recovered or identified: the corpse seen in the French Broad was only 'supposed' to be his (A2). The only stated motive was a later Raleigh report that he was lynched 'for an alleged assault upon a negro woman' (A3).
The core account came from one witness, Henry Sumner, in a single Raleigh telegram (A1); the later reports add only an unidentified floating body and a 'supposed' link to the case (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Henry Sumner's account (Raleigh telegram)
accounts.gist: Two white men quarreled with three Black women; one knocked down Lottie Corpening, the women attacked the men, and five Black men then beat the man who could not flee and took him away with a rope.

accounts.label: Asheville report of the floating body
accounts.gist: A white man's body seen in the French Broad on August 22 was 'supposed' to be the lynched man; it was not recovered.

accounts.label: Later Raleigh telegram
accounts.gist: The 'current belief' was that the body was that of the man lynched by Black men 'for an alleged assault upon a negro woman'.

framing.detail: The Dispatch ran the story under 'A LYNCHING' in a Raleigh news roundup, relaying Sumner's account and stressing that the attackers were 'negroes'.
The Asheville Citizen headlined 'A SENSATION' and 'Supposed to be the Man that was Lynched by Negroes in Henderson County', calling the Black witnesses 'darkies'.
The Dispatch's follow-up, 'A MYSTERIOUS CORPSE IN THE FRENCH BROAD', gave the motive as 'an alleged assault upon a negro woman'.

versions.value: A quarrel in which one white man knocked down Lottie Corpening, after which the women and then the five men attacked

conflicts.note: The versions are compatible (knocking down a woman is an assault), but only A3 frames it as the reason for the lynching; A1 is the fuller and earlier account.

versions.value: Arms appeared tied down to the trunk (Lyda and Weldon; Dispatch: hands appeared tied)
Arms and hands sticking up out of the water (Davis)

conflicts.note: Eyewitnesses at Asheville differed; the body was never recovered or identified.
